name: Riesling

lines.s10: Riesling is the white of the Mosel and the Rhine: lime, green apple and white peach on piercing acidity, dry or sweet.
lines.s20: Riesling comes from Germany's river valleys, and it can be bone dry, gently sweet or richly sweet. In every style it tastes of lime, green apple and white peach, with no taste of oak and an acidity that keeps it fresh for decades.
lines.s45: Riesling is the white that hides nothing: no oak and no cream, only the fruit and the place. Its home is Germany, on the steep slate banks of the Mosel and along the Rhine. It tastes of lime, green apple and white peach, and with years in bottle it gains a note like petrol. It is light, with piercing acidity, and it runs from bone dry to honey sweet. Germany often leaves a touch of sweetness at low alcohol, while Australia ferments it fully dry. Pour it with crab, smoked trout or anything with chilli. The first record of it is a bill for vines dated 1435.
lines.sale: Riesling brings lime, green apple and an acidity that makes the next bite taste brighter. I would pour an off dry one with anything that carries heat, and a dry one with the crab.

glass.lead: Lime, green apple and white peach over wet slate, light and unoaked, with piercing acidity and a petrol note with age.

ladder.where: The Mosel, the Rheingau and the Nahe; the Finger Lakes
The Pfalz, the Wachau and Washington's Columbia Valley
The Clare Valley, where hot days meet cold nights

glass.structure: Dry to sweet. Acidity high, alcohol low where sugar is left and moderate when dry, body light to medium; no new oak.

old.where: Germany's Mosel, Rheingau and Pfalz; Alsace; Austria's Wachau
old.glass: The Mosel tends to be feather light and often off dry: lime, green apple and white peach over wet slate, at low alcohol. Alsace, the Pfalz and the Wachau are usually dry and fuller.
old.cellar: Fermented in steel or in large, old oak casks that add no flavour; in Germany the fermentation is often stopped early to keep a little natural sweetness.

new.where: South Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys, the Finger Lakes, Washington, New Zealand
new.glass: Clare and Eden Valley are typically bone dry and vivid: lime juice, lemon zest and a steely edge at moderate alcohol, with toast and petrol often showing early. The Finger Lakes and Washington range from dry to sweet.
new.cellar: Usually fermented cold in steel, kept away from oak and air, and bottled early under screwcap; Australia ferments it fully dry.

contrast.why: Germany's river valleys sit near the northern limit for ripening, so sugar stays low and a little sweetness balances the acidity; its law grades grapes by ripeness. Australia's sunnier sites ripen fully, and the wine is fermented dry.
contrast.blur: Germany now bottles much of its Riesling dry, labelled trocken, and the Finger Lakes and New Zealand make light, off dry wines in the Mosel manner.
contrast.call: Sweetness at low alcohol, or peach on a fuller dry frame, leans Old World; taut, bone dry lime with early toast or petrol leans Australia.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; the sweet wines a little colder.
service.glass: A white wine glass with a narrow bowl; a small glass for the sweet wines.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; pour gently and leave any harmless crystals in the bottle.
service.age: It keeps longer than almost any other white: sound dry wines ten years or more, the sweet wines for decades.

with.dish: Thai or Vietnamese dishes with chilli
with.why: a touch of sweetness and low alcohol soften the heat
bright acidity lifts the sweet meat
acidity cuts the oil and the smoke
off dry fruit cools the cayenne, acidity cuts the butter

labels.means: Dry, on a German label; halbtrocken and feinherb are off dry.
German grades of ripeness at harvest, in rising order; a Kabinett or a Spätlese may be dry or sweet.
A dry wine from a classed vineyard of the VDP, a German growers' association; often written GG.

guest.a: No. It runs from bone dry to very sweet. On a German label trocken means dry, and wines from Alsace, Austria and Australia are mostly dry.

guest.q: Why does this one smell of petrol?
guest.a: That is a mark of the grape, not a fault. It builds with years in bottle and shows sooner in wines from hot, sunny sites. Many Riesling drinkers look for it.

guest.q: How can I tell from the label whether it is dry?
guest.a: Look for trocken on a German bottle, and check the alcohol: near eight or nine per cent means sugar was left, and twelve or more is usually dry.

compare.tell: Chenin Blanc shows quince, honey and a wet wool note on a broader, waxier frame; Riesling is lime and petrol, lighter and more piercing.
Grüner Veltliner brings white pepper, lentil and celery; dry Riesling is lime, white peach and, with age, petrol, with no peppery note.
Albariño is salty, with peach, apricot and a faintly bitter finish; Riesling has higher acidity, lime and wet slate, and may carry sweetness.

cards.front: Riesling: where is it at home, and what is its first record?
cards.back: Germany, above all the Mosel and the Rhine. A cellar account of 13 March 1435 records Riesling vines bought at Rüsselsheim on the Main, near the Rheingau.

cards.front: Riesling blind: the Mosel or the Clare Valley, what tips it?
cards.back: Sweetness, low alcohol and wet slate lean Mosel. Bone dry lime juice at moderate alcohol, with toast or petrol showing early, leans Clare or Eden Valley.

cards.front: On a German Riesling label, what do trocken and Kabinett tell you?
cards.back: Trocken means dry. Kabinett is the first grade of ripeness at harvest, and it may be dry or carry sweetness; low alcohol hints at sugar left in the wine.

questions.q: A blind white is young, pale, bone dry and vivid: lime juice, lemon zest and a touch of toast, with high acidity, moderate alcohol and no oak. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Bone dry lime juice with toast showing young, at moderate alcohol, is the Clare Valley's way with Riesling. A typical Mosel wine is lighter, lower in alcohol and often off dry.

questions.q: A guest loves German Riesling but wants no sweetness at all. Which word on the label tells you the bottle is dry?
questions.exp: Trocken means dry. Feinherb is off dry, and Spätlese and Auslese are grades of ripeness that usually carry sweetness unless trocken is printed beside them.

questions.q: A guest sniffs a ten year old Riesling and asks, worried, why it smells of petrol. What do you tell her?
opts: It is a normal mark of aged Riesling
The wine is corked and must be replaced
The bottle was stored beside fuel
It comes from ageing in new oak
questions.exp: A petrol note builds in Riesling with bottle age, and sooner from hot, sunny sites; it is no fault. Cork taint smells of damp cardboard, and Riesling sees no new oak.

sources.title: Wines of Germany: Riesling, Germany's white star
wein.plus Magazine: first mention of the Riesling is celebrated worldwide

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it: Germany, Alsace and the Wachau against the Clare and Eden Valleys, the Finger Lakes and Washington.
The say line is the Court's own, REES-ling.
The first record, 13 March 1435 at Rüsselsheim, stands on the German Wine Institute, which keeps that day as the grape's birthday; the count who bought the vines is not named.

The ladder calls the Clare Valley warm, as the Codex's own region record does (hot days giving way to cold nights) and as the Régionale row says of petrol showing young there; the Eden Valley is higher and cooler and is left off the ladder.
Age agrees with the tasting dial, which says Riesling ages further than any other white, softened here to almost any other.
Left out: the parentage (Gouais Blanc and a Traminer cross), since the Chardonnay pilot already closes on Gouais Blanc; the Spätlese story of 1775 at Johannisberg, which would name an estate.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
